title: Level 3 – Global Nurse Professional
subtitle: Creating Safe Healthcare Environments
intro: Program Outline Welcome to the highest level of the GNPS learning pathway. Global Nursing Professionals do more than follow safety procedures. They lead improvements, analyse patterns of harm, strengthen systems, mentor colleagues and help create healthcare environments in which safety is a shared organisational value. This level develops advanced capability in safety leadership, quality improvement, infection surveillance, human factors, systems thinking, digital health and global collaboration. It prepares nurses to influence practice beyond the care of an individual patient. What You Will Learn Throughout this level you will strengthen your ability to: 1. Lead a culture of safety, openness and continuous learning 2. Analyse incidents using systems and human-factors approaches 3. Design and evaluate quality-improvement initiatives 4. Use surveillance data to strengthen infection prevention 5. Promote antimicrobial stewardship and responsible clinical practice 6. Apply digital technologies safely and ethically 7. Support workforce wellbeing, resilience and psychological safety 8. Lead preparedness for outbreaks, disasters and emerging risks 9. Contribute to global learning and sustainable healthcare improvement Why This Learning Matters Healthcare harm rarely results from one person's action alone. It often arises from weaknesses in communication, workflow, technology, staffing, policy or organisational culture. Global Nursing Professionals recognise these connections and lead practical improvements that make safe practice easier for everyone. Your Learning Goal By completing Level 3, you should be prepared to lead safety and quality initiatives, use data and evidence to improve systems, support colleagues and contribute to safer healthcare locally and globally.

sections.title: Leading a Culture of Safety and Psychological Safety

content.text: Safety culture reflects the values and behaviours that determine how an organisation responds to risk, error and improvement. Nurse leaders influence culture through their daily actions: whether they listen to concerns, respond fairly, support learning and model the standards expected of others.
Learning outcomes

items: Describe the characteristics of a positive safety culture
Promote psychological safety within healthcare teams
Apply just-culture principles when responding to incidents
Model professional accountability and learning

content.text: Safety Culture A strong safety culture makes it normal to report hazards, question unsafe decisions and learn from incidents. Leaders communicate that safety is a priority even when workload is high. Policies are supported by staffing, equipment, education and visible leadership behaviour.

Psychological Safety Team members need confidence that they can ask questions, admit uncertainty and raise concerns without humiliation. Psychological safety does not remove accountability. It enables early communication so that mistakes can be prevented or corrected.

Just Culture A just culture distinguishes human error, at-risk behaviour and reckless behaviour. Human error may require system redesign and support; at-risk behaviour requires coaching and removal of incentives for shortcuts; reckless disregard requires proportionate accountability. Automatic blame discourages reporting, while absence of accountability also damages safety.

Leadership Presence Leaders strengthen trust by responding promptly, following through on reported concerns and explaining decisions. Staff quickly notice when safety messages are not matched by action.

A junior nurse reports connecting a feeding tube incorrectly but identifies the problem before use. The manager first confirms patient safety, thanks the nurse for reporting and reviews the equipment, training and workflow. The review identifies confusing connectors and interruptions during preparation. The team introduces a standard setup and simulation practice rather than treating the event only as individual carelessness.
Key learning points

items: Make speaking up safe and expected
Respond to reports with fairness and curiosity
Match accountability to behaviour and context
Demonstrate through action that safety concerns matter

sections.title: Using Systems Thinking and Human Factors to Prevent Harm

content.text: Healthcare is a complex system in which people, equipment, technology, workload, environment and procedures interact. Systems thinking looks beyond the final action to understand why the conditions for error developed. Human-factors principles help redesign work so that safe actions are easier and errors are more difficult.
Learning outcomes

items: Analyse incidents beyond individual blame
Identify human and system factors that contribute to risk
Use root-cause and contributory-factor approaches
Recommend practical system controls

content.text: Systems Thinking When an error occurs, the visible action may be only the final point in a longer chain. Staffing shortages, look-alike packaging, poor lighting, interruptions, unclear responsibility or inaccessible guidance may all contribute. Effective review asks what happened, how it happened and what conditions made it possible.

Human Factors People have limits in memory, attention and perception. Safe systems do not depend on perfect concentration. Standardisation, clear labelling, forcing functions, checklists, reduced interruptions and well-designed technology can support performance.

Hierarchy of Controls Education and reminders are useful but often weak when used alone. Stronger controls include removing the hazard, substituting safer equipment, redesigning processes, introducing engineering safeguards and then supporting these measures with policy and training.

Learning Reviews Incident analysis should involve the people who understand the work, including frontline staff and where appropriate patients. Recommendations should be specific, assigned, monitored and evaluated rather than ending with a general instruction to 'be more careful'.

A unit experiences repeated wrong-selection errors involving two injectable medicines with similar packaging. A systems review identifies adjacent storage, similar labels, frequent interruptions and an electronic search that displays both names together. The response includes separated storage, warning labels, barcode safeguards and redesign of the electronic display, supported by staff education.
Key learning points

items: Look for conditions that shaped the error
Design systems for normal human limitations
Prefer stronger controls over reminders alone
Monitor whether recommendations actually reduce risk

sections.title: Quality Improvement, Surveillance and Antimicrobial Stewardship

content.text: Global Nursing Professionals use data to identify patterns, test improvements and evaluate outcomes. Infection surveillance, clinical audits, patient feedback and incident trends turn everyday observations into organised learning. Nurses also contribute to antimicrobial stewardship by preventing infection and supporting appropriate use of antimicrobial medicines.
Learning outcomes

items: Use data to define a safety or infection-prevention problem
Apply a structured quality-improvement cycle
Interpret process and outcome measures
Explain the nursing contribution to antimicrobial stewardship

content.text: Quality-Improvement Cycles Improvement begins by defining a specific problem and understanding current practice. Teams then introduce a focused change, study the results and adapt the intervention. Small tests of change allow learning before wider implementation.

Measurement Outcome measures show what happened, such as infection or fall rates. Process measures show whether recommended care occurred, such as hand-hygiene compliance or timely device review. Balancing measures identify unintended effects, such as delays or increased workload.

Surveillance and Feedback Surveillance identifies trends by location, organism, procedure or device. Data become useful when they are timely, reliable and communicated to the people who can act. Feedback should support improvement rather than simply publish performance figures.

Antimicrobial Stewardship Nurses support stewardship by obtaining cultures correctly, administering antimicrobials at the prescribed time, monitoring response and adverse effects, checking allergy information, educating patients and questioning unnecessary continuation through appropriate channels. Preventing infection reduces the need for antimicrobial treatment.

A ward records an increase in catheter-associated urinary infections. The improvement team maps the process and finds that catheter necessity is not reviewed consistently. Nurses introduce a daily review prompt, removal criteria and feedback dashboard. They monitor infection rates, catheter days and any unintended need for reinsertion. The intervention is adjusted after each review cycle.
Key learning points

items: Define the problem before choosing the solution
Measure both outcomes and care processes
Use feedback to support local action
Infection prevention and stewardship are closely connected

sections.title: Digital Safety, Preparedness and Global Collaboration

content.text: Modern safety practice extends beyond the physical ward. Electronic records, clinical decision support, remote monitoring and connected devices can improve care but also introduce new risks. Global Nursing Professionals must use technology critically, protect information and contribute to preparedness for outbreaks, disasters and emerging health threats.
Learning outcomes

items: Identify benefits and risks of digital healthcare systems
Promote safe use of electronic records and connected devices
Contribute to outbreak and emergency preparedness
Share learning across organisations and countries

content.text: Digital Clinical Safety Technology can reduce transcription errors, highlight allergies and improve access to information. However, incorrect data, alert fatigue, copied documentation, system downtime and automation bias can create harm. Nurses should verify critical information and report technology-related hazards.

Information Governance Patient information must be accessed only for legitimate care purposes and protected through secure passwords, appropriate screen use and careful communication. Digital convenience does not reduce the duty of confidentiality.

Preparedness and Resilience Outbreaks and disasters require clear roles, communication pathways, PPE availability, triage processes, staff support and continuity plans. Preparedness should be practised through education and simulation rather than created only after an emergency begins.

Global Collaboration Infection and safety threats cross borders. Nurses contribute by sharing surveillance information, adapting evidence to local contexts, participating in professional networks and learning from different health systems. Global collaboration should respect local resources and avoid assuming that one solution fits every setting.

During a respiratory outbreak, a hospital introduces remote monitoring to reduce unnecessary room entry. Nurse leaders identify that alarm thresholds are generating too many non-urgent alerts. They work with clinicians and technical staff to adjust the system, maintain direct assessment for concerning patients and establish a downtime plan. Technology supports care without replacing professional judgement.
Key learning points

items: Technology supports but does not replace clinical judgement
Protect confidentiality in every digital interaction
Preparedness requires planning, practice and workforce support
Share global learning while adapting solutions to local needs

content.text: End-of-Program Summary By completing GNPS Program 2 – Level 3, you have developed the advanced perspective of a Global Nursing Professional. You are prepared not only to follow safe practice but also to lead culture, analyse systems, use data, support innovation and contribute to resilient healthcare environments. Protecting patients and protecting the workforce are shared responsibilities that require knowledge, courage, collaboration and continuous learning.
